extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians, comedy writers, and humorists learning joke craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for writing and evaluating observational stand-up jokes in the style of Jerry Seinfeld, emphasizing specificity, word choice, pacing, and live testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and Relatability
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on specific images and emotions around an experience so the observation feels concrete and familiar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid, narrowly observed details (example: the dread inspired by the hinges on a portable toilet door, the lasting mental scarring from seeing contents) that are both specific and universally relatable. Aim for observations that people recognize from their own lives so they connect immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funny Word Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose words for their sound and comedic value; some words are intrinsically funnier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for short words and words with hard consonants (K sounds especially). Prefer punchy, monosyllabic or brief words ('chimps', 'dirt', 'playing', 'sticks') over long, soft words. Word-level sound choices contribute to immediacy and laugh potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and Word Crafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Every word must earn its place; trim sentences and words until they are precisely right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid jokes that are too long or too short. 'Shave off' letters or syllables and count syllables to tighten rhythm. Continuously edit to remove excess words; if a word or syllable can be cut without losing meaning or impact, cut it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression and Pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Place jokes close together and control pacing so laughter builds rather than dissipates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compression triggers 'the roll': deliver one joke quickly after another to compound laughs. Structure sequences so each joke propels the next and the audience doesn't stop laughing between beats. Pay attention to timing and transitions to maintain momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke Structure (Cliff Metaphor: setup → punchline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the setup as the cliff edge of expectation and the punchline as the landing on the other side; the audience must make that mental leap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly establish the setup's endpoint (the 'cliff') so the punchline can provide a surprising, coherent resolution on the other side. If the leap is unclear, some audience members 'fall into the ravine' (miss the joke). Ensure the relationship between setup and punchline is sharply defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing & Performance Testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Live performance and iterative editing are essential; refine jokes based on audience reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test material in front of live audiences, closely observe responses, and adjust wording, timing, and pacing accordingly. Be prepared to spend long periods—sometimes years—fine-tuning a single joke. Use performance feedback as the primary metric for whether changes improve laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelism and Rhythmic Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parallel sentence structure to create rhythm and set up expectations that can be subverted for laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ parallel constructions (example: 'Two in a packet … and … two slots in the toaster') to build a predictable rhythm that enhances the punch when it deviates. Parallelism helps with timing and audience anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seinfeld-style Joke Evaluation Checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A concise rubric of questions to evaluate whether a joke meets Seinfeld's principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these evaluation prompts: 1) Is the observation maximally specific and relatable? 2) Are the words chosen for sound (short, hard consonants)? 3) Is every word essential—could any be cut? 4) Does it pace well in a sequence (compression)? 5) Is the setup clearly establishing a 'cliff edge' of expectation? 6) Does the punchline land cleanly on the other side? 7) Is there parallel structure for rhythm? Apply these sequentially while testing and editing onstage.
